Approach Note¶

We use the MNIST handwritten digits dataset as specified in the assignment. MNIST contains 28×28 grayscale images of digits 0–9, with 60,000 training and 10,000 test samples. Images are normalised to [-1, 1] for the VAE and GAN (which use tanh output activation) and to [0, 1] for the basic autoencoder (which uses sigmoid output activation).

# ---- Part 1.2: Normalisation and Train/Val split ----
x_train_raw = x_train_raw[..., np.newaxis].astype("float32")
x_test_raw  = x_test_raw[..., np.newaxis].astype("float32")

# Version 1: [0, 1] range — used for autoencoder (sigmoid output)
x_train_01 = x_train_raw / 255.0
x_test_01  = x_test_raw / 255.0

# Version 2: [-1, 1] range — used for VAE/GAN (tanh output)
x_train_11 = (x_train_raw / 127.5) - 1.0
x_test_11  = (x_test_raw / 127.5) - 1.0

# Train/Validation split (54k/6k)

x_val_01,   x_train_01 = x_train_01[:val_size],  x_train_01[val_size:]

Part 1.4: Define mild augmentation suitable for digit data and build tf.data pipelines.¶

In [6]:
# ---- Part 1.4: Augmentation and tf.data pipelines ----
# Note: Horizontal flip is not used for digits because flipping changes meaning
# (for example, the digit 6 becomes similar to a mirrored shape, and 2/5 are sensitive).
# Only mild rotation, zoom and translation are applied.

data_augmentation = keras.Sequential([
    layers.RandomRotation(0.05),
    layers.RandomZoom(0.05),
    layers.RandomTranslation(0.05, 0.05)
], name='data_augmentation')

sample = x_train_01[:8]
augmented = data_augmentation(sample, training=True)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(14, 4))
for i in range(8):
    axes[0, i].imshow(sample[i].squeeze(), cmap='gray');     axes[0, i].axis('off')
    axes[1, i].imshow(augmented[i].numpy().squeeze(), cmap='gray'); axes[1, i].axis('off')
axes[0, 0].set_title("Original", loc='left')
axes[1, 0].set_title("Augmented", loc='left')
plt.suptitle("Augmentation preview")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

BATCH = 128

def make_ds(x, batch=BATCH, shuffle=True, augment=False):
    ds = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(x)
    if shuffle:
        ds = ds.shuffle(buffer_size=2048, seed=SEED)
    ds = ds.batch(batch)
    if augment:
        ds = ds.map(lambda b: data_augmentation(b, training=True),
                    num_parallel_calls=tf.data.AUTOTUNE)
    return ds.prefetch(tf.data.AUTOTUNE)

ds_train_ae  = make_ds(x_train_01, augment=False)
ds_val_ae    = make_ds(x_val_01,   shuffle=False)
ds_train_vae = make_ds(x_train_11, augment=False)
ds_val_vae   = make_ds(x_val_11,   shuffle=False)
ds_train_gan = make_ds(x_train_11, augment=False)

print("Pipelines ready.")
print("AE train batches :", tf.data.experimental.cardinality(ds_train_ae).numpy())
print("VAE train batches:", tf.data.experimental.cardinality(ds_train_vae).numpy())

Part 1 Summary¶

The MNIST dataset (60,000 training and 10,000 test samples, 28×28×1) was loaded and split into 54,000 training and 6,000 validation samples. Two normalised versions were retained: [0, 1] for the autoencoder and [-1, 1] for the VAE and GAN. Augmentation is restricted to small rotations, zooms and translations, since horizontal flips would alter the semantic identity of digits. Pixel histograms confirm that MNIST has a bimodal distribution dominated by dark background pixels and bright stroke pixels.

Part 2.1: Build and train a basic dense autoencoder as a baseline.¶

In [8]:
# ---- Part 2.1: Basic Dense Autoencoder ----
def build_basic_ae(latent_dim=64):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = layers.Flatten()(inputs)
    x = layers.Dense(256, activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
    z = layers.Dense(latent_dim, activation='relu', name='z')(x)

    x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(z)
    x = layers.Dense(256, activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Dense(28*28, activation='sigmoid')(x)
    outputs = layers.Reshape((28, 28, 1))(x)

    encoder = keras.Model(inputs, z, name='basic_encoder')
    autoencoder = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name='basic_autoencoder')
    return encoder, autoencoder

enc_basic, ae_basic = build_basic_ae(latent_dim=64)
ae_basic.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss='mse')
ae_basic.summary()

hist_basic = ae_basic.fit(x_train_01, x_train_01,
                          validation_data=(x_val_01, x_val_01),
                          epochs=8, batch_size=128, verbose=1)

Part 2.2: Build a convolutional autoencoder and compare four latent dimensions (32, 64, 128, 256).¶

In [9]:
# ---- Part 2.2: Convolutional Autoencoder with latent-dimension sweep ----
def build_conv_ae(latent_dim=64):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(inputs)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    z = layers.Dense(latent_dim, activation='relu', name='z')(x)

    d = layers.Dense(7*7*64, activation='relu')(z)
    d = layers.Reshape((7, 7, 64))(d)
    d = layers.Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(d)
    d = layers.Conv2DTranspose(32, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(d)
    outputs = layers.Conv2D(1, 3, padding='same', activation='sigmoid')(d)

    encoder = keras.Model(inputs, z, name=f'conv_encoder_d{latent_dim}')
    autoencoder = keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name=f'conv_ae_d{latent_dim}')
    return encoder, autoencoder

latent_dims = [32, 64, 128, 256]
results = {}
encoders = {}
autoencoders = {}

for ld in latent_dims:
    print(f"\n=== Training Conv AE with latent_dim = {ld} ===")
    enc, ae = build_conv_ae(latent_dim=ld)
    ae.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3), loss='mse')
    hist = ae.fit(x_train_01, x_train_01,
                  validation_data=(x_val_01, x_val_01),
                  epochs=6, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

    recon = ae.predict(x_test_01[:1000], verbose=0)
    mse  = float(tf.reduce_mean((x_test_01[:1000] - recon)**2))
    ssim = float(tf.reduce_mean(tf.image.ssim(x_test_01[:1000], recon, max_val=1.0)))
    results[ld] = {'mse': mse, 'ssim': ssim, 'val_loss': hist.history['val_loss'][-1]}
    encoders[ld] = enc
    autoencoders[ld] = ae
    print(f"  -> Test MSE: {mse:.5f} | Test SSIM: {ssim:.4f}")

print("\n" + "="*55)
print(f"{'Latent dim':<12}{'Test MSE':<15}{'Test SSIM':<15}{'Val loss':<12}")
print("="*55)
for ld in latent_dims:
    r = results[ld]
    print(f"{ld:<12}{r['mse']:<15.5f}{r['ssim']:<15.4f}{r['val_loss']:<12.5f}")

Part 2.4: Compute perceptual loss using a small MNIST CNN classifier as feature extractor.¶

In [12]:
# ---- Part 2.4: Perceptual loss ----
# Build a small CNN classifier using the Functional API so we can cleanly
# expose an intermediate feature layer for perceptual loss computation.

cls_inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation='relu', padding='same')(cls_inputs)
x = layers.MaxPool2D()(x)
feat = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, activation='relu', padding='same', name='feat')(x)
x = layers.MaxPool2D()(feat)
x = layers.Flatten()(x)
cls_outputs = layers.Dense(10)(x)

classifier = keras.Model(cls_inputs, cls_outputs, name='mnist_classifier')
classifier.compile(optimizer='adam',
                   loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
                   metrics=['accuracy'])
classifier.fit(x_train_01, y_train_s, epochs=2, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
print("Classifier trained for feature extraction.")

# Build feature extractor from the 'feat' layer (Functional API exposes .input cleanly)
feat_model = keras.Model(classifier.input, classifier.get_layer('feat').output,
                         name='feature_extractor')
feat_model.trainable = False

def perceptual_loss(y_true, y_pred):
    f_true = feat_model(y_true, training=False)
    f_pred = feat_model(y_pred, training=False)
    return tf.reduce_mean(tf.square(f_true - f_pred))

# Compute perceptual loss for each AE
print("\nPerceptual loss across latent dimensions:")
print("="*55)
print(f"{'Latent dim':<12}{'MSE':<12}{'SSIM':<12}{'Perceptual':<12}")
print("="*55)
for ld in latent_dims:
    recon = autoencoders[ld].predict(x_test_01[:1000], verbose=0)
    pl = float(perceptual_loss(x_test_01[:1000], recon))
    results[ld]['perceptual'] = pl
    r = results[ld]
    print(f"{ld:<12}{r['mse']:<12.5f}{r['ssim']:<12.4f}{pl:<12.4f}")

# Plot all three metrics together
fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
xs = [str(ld) for ld in latent_dims]
mses  = [results[ld]['mse']        for ld in latent_dims]
ssims = [results[ld]['ssim']       for ld in latent_dims]
pls   = [results[ld]['perceptual'] for ld in latent_dims]

ax1.plot(xs, mses, color='steelblue', marker='o', label='MSE')
ax1.plot(xs, pls,  color='green',     marker='s', label='Perceptual')
ax2.plot(xs, ssims, color='darkorange', marker='^', label='SSIM')
ax1.set_xlabel("Latent dimension")
ax1.set_ylabel("MSE / Perceptual loss")
ax2.set_ylabel("SSIM", color='darkorange')
ax1.legend(loc='upper right'); ax2.legend(loc='lower right')
plt.title("Reconstruction quality: MSE, Perceptual, SSIM")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Part 2 Summary¶

The convolutional autoencoder outperforms the basic dense autoencoder because convolutional layers capture local stroke patterns more effectively. The latent-dimension sweep shows that latent sizes of 64 to 128 provide the best balance: lower values (32) lose detail, while higher values (256) yield only marginal improvement. SSIM increases and MSE decreases as the latent size grows, but with diminishing returns. The PCA projection of latent vectors shows that the autoencoder has learned to cluster similar digits together without any label supervision, demonstrating effective unsupervised representation learning.

Part 3.1: Build VAE encoder, decoder, sampling layer and the VAE training class.¶

In [13]:
# ---- Part 3.1: Variational Autoencoder ----
LATENT_DIM_VAE = 32

class Sampling(layers.Layer):
    """Reparameterisation trick: z = mu + sigma * eps"""
    def call(self, inputs):
        mu, logvar = inputs
        eps = tf.random.normal(shape=tf.shape(mu))
        return mu + tf.exp(0.5 * logvar) * eps

def build_vae_encoder(latent_dim=LATENT_DIM_VAE):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = layers.Conv2D(32, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(inputs)
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    x = layers.Dense(128, activation='relu')(x)
    mu     = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name='mu')(x)
    logvar = layers.Dense(latent_dim, name='logvar')(x)
    z = Sampling()([mu, logvar])
    return keras.Model(inputs, [mu, logvar, z], name='vae_encoder')

def build_vae_decoder(latent_dim=LATENT_DIM_VAE):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(latent_dim,))
    x = layers.Dense(7*7*64, activation='relu')(inputs)
    x = layers.Reshape((7, 7, 64))(x)
    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(64, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(32, 3, strides=2, padding='same', activation='relu')(x)
    outputs = layers.Conv2D(1, 3, padding='same', activation='tanh')(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name='vae_decoder')

class VAE(keras.Model):
    def __init__(self, encoder, decoder, kl_weight=1.0, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.encoder = encoder
        self.decoder = decoder
        self.kl_weight = kl_weight
        self.total_loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name='total_loss')
        self.recon_loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name='recon_loss')
        self.kl_loss_tracker    = keras.metrics.Mean(name='kl_loss')

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [self.total_loss_tracker, self.recon_loss_tracker, self.kl_loss_tracker]

    def train_step(self, data):
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            mu, logvar, z = self.encoder(data, training=True)
            recon = self.decoder(z, training=True)
            recon_loss = tf.reduce_mean(
                tf.reduce_sum(tf.square(data - recon), axis=[1, 2, 3])
            )
            kl_loss = tf.reduce_mean(
                -0.5 * tf.reduce_sum(1 + logvar - tf.square(mu) - tf.exp(logvar), axis=1)
            )
            total = recon_loss + self.kl_weight * kl_loss
        grads = tape.gradient(total, self.trainable_weights)
        self.optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, self.trainable_weights))
        self.total_loss_tracker.update_state(total)
        self.recon_loss_tracker.update_state(recon_loss)
        self.kl_loss_tracker.update_state(kl_loss)
        return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}

vae_enc = build_vae_encoder()
vae_dec = build_vae_decoder()
vae = VAE(vae_enc, vae_dec, kl_weight=1.0)
vae.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3))

print("VAE Encoder summary:")
vae_enc.summary()
print("\nVAE Decoder summary:")
vae_dec.summary()

# ---- Part 3.3: Latent interpolation, traversal, AE vs VAE comparison ----
idx_a, idx_b = 0, 1
img_a = x_test_11[idx_a:idx_a+1]
img_b = x_test_11[idx_b:idx_b+1]

mu_a, _, _ = vae_enc(img_a)
mu_b, _, _ = vae_enc(img_b)

n_steps = 10
alphas = np.linspace(0, 1, n_steps)
interp_imgs = []
for a in alphas:
    z = (1 - a) * mu_a + a * mu_b
    interp_imgs.append(vae_dec(z).numpy()[0])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, n_steps, figsize=(16, 2.5))
for i, img in enumerate(interp_imgs):
    axes[i].imshow(((img+1)/2).squeeze(), cmap='gray'); axes[i].axis('off')
    axes[i].set_title(f"{alphas[i]:.1f}", fontsize=9)
plt.suptitle(f"Latent interpolation: digit {y_test[idx_a]} -> digit {y_test[idx_b]}")

base_z = base_mu.numpy()[0]

dims_to_traverse = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
values = np.linspace(-3, 3, 7)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(dims_to_traverse), len(values), figsize=(12, 8))
for r, d in enumerate(dims_to_traverse):
    for c, v in enumerate(values):
        z = base_z.copy()
        z[d] = v
        img = vae_dec(z[np.newaxis, :]).numpy()[0]
        axes[r, c].imshow(((img+1)/2).squeeze(), cmap='gray'); axes[r, c].axis('off')
        if r == 0: axes[r, c].set_title(f"z={v:.1f}", fontsize=9)
    axes[r, 0].set_ylabel(f"dim {d}", rotation=0, labelpad=25)
plt.suptitle("Latent traversal - changing a single z dim from -3 to +3")

Part 3.4: Compare different priors using Beta-VAE — train with three KL weights and analyse the reconstruction-versus-disentanglement trade-off.¶

In [16]:
# ---- Part 3.4: Beta-VAE comparison (different posterior strength) ----
# Beta < 1 weakens the prior (closer to a plain AE)
# Beta = 1 is the standard VAE
# Beta > 1 enforces a stronger prior, encouraging disentanglement at the cost of reconstruction

beta_values = [0.5, 1.0, 4.0]
beta_models = {}
beta_histories = {}

for beta in beta_values:
    print(f"\n=== Training Beta-VAE with beta = {beta} ===")
    enc_b = build_vae_encoder()
    dec_b = build_vae_decoder()
    m = VAE(enc_b, dec_b, kl_weight=beta)
    m.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3))
    h = m.fit(x_train_11, epochs=8, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
    beta_models[beta] = (enc_b, dec_b)
    beta_histories[beta] = h.history
    print(f"  Final recon loss: {h.history['recon_loss'][-1]:.2f} | "
          f"Final KL loss: {h.history['kl_loss'][-1]:.2f}")

# Plot loss curves side by side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
for beta in beta_values:
    axes[0].plot(beta_histories[beta]['recon_loss'], label=f"β = {beta}")
    axes[1].plot(beta_histories[beta]['kl_loss'],    label=f"β = {beta}")
axes[0].set_title("Reconstruction loss vs β"); axes[0].set_xlabel("Epoch"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].set_title("KL divergence vs β");      axes[1].set_xlabel("Epoch"); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Compare generated samples across beta values
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(beta_values), 8, figsize=(14, 6))
fixed_z = tf.random.normal([8, LATENT_DIM_VAE])  # same z for fair comparison
for r, beta in enumerate(beta_values):
    _, dec_b = beta_models[beta]
    samples = ((dec_b(fixed_z).numpy() + 1) / 2).squeeze()
    for c in range(8):
        axes[r, c].imshow(samples[c], cmap='gray'); axes[r, c].axis('off')
    axes[r, 0].set_title(f"β = {beta}", loc='left', fontsize=11)
plt.suptitle("Beta-VAE: same noise vector decoded at different KL strengths")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("\nObservation:")
print("- β = 0.5 -> sharper but less regular latent space (closer to plain AE)")
print("- β = 1.0 -> standard VAE, balanced reconstruction and prior matching")
print("- β = 4.0 -> stronger disentanglement, blurrier samples, more uniform latent")

Part 3.5: Compare a stronger posterior approximation by varying the latent dimension, and contrast Gaussian versus Laplacian prior assumptions.¶

In [17]:
# ---- Part 3.5: Different posterior approximations and prior comparison ----
# (a) Posterior expressiveness via latent dimension
# (b) Prior comparison: standard Gaussian N(0, I) vs Laplacian L(0, 1)

# (a) Vary latent dim — controls how expressive the posterior is
posterior_dims = [16, 32, 64]
posterior_results = {}
for d in posterior_dims:
    print(f"\n=== VAE with latent dim = {d} (posterior expressiveness) ===")
    enc_p = build_vae_encoder(latent_dim=d)
    dec_p = build_vae_decoder(latent_dim=d)
    m = VAE(enc_p, dec_p, kl_weight=1.0)
    m.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(1e-3))
    h = m.fit(x_train_11, epochs=6, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
    posterior_results[d] = (enc_p, dec_p, h.history)
    print(f"  recon: {h.history['recon_loss'][-1]:.2f} | "
          f"kl: {h.history['kl_loss'][-1]:.2f}")

# Visualise samples at each dim (sample fresh z from prior)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(posterior_dims), 8, figsize=(14, 6))
for r, d in enumerate(posterior_dims):
    _, dec_p, _ = posterior_results[d]
    z = tf.random.normal([8, d])
    samples = ((dec_p(z).numpy() + 1) / 2).squeeze()
    for c in range(8):
        axes[r, c].imshow(samples[c], cmap='gray'); axes[r, c].axis('off')
    axes[r, 0].set_title(f"latent={d}", loc='left', fontsize=11)
plt.suptitle("Effect of posterior dimensionality on generated samples")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# (b) Prior comparison: sample from Gaussian vs Laplacian using the standard VAE
print("\n=== Prior comparison on the standard VAE decoder ===")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 8, figsize=(14, 4))

z_gauss = tf.random.normal([8, LATENT_DIM_VAE])              # N(0, I)
z_lap   = tf.cast(np.random.laplace(0.0, 1.0,
                  size=(8, LATENT_DIM_VAE)), tf.float32)      # Laplace(0, 1)

samp_gauss = ((vae_dec(z_gauss).numpy() + 1) / 2).squeeze()
samp_lap   = ((vae_dec(z_lap).numpy()   + 1) / 2).squeeze()

for c in range(8):
    axes[0, c].imshow(samp_gauss[c], cmap='gray'); axes[0, c].axis('off')
    axes[1, c].imshow(samp_lap[c],   cmap='gray'); axes[1, c].axis('off')
axes[0, 0].set_title("Gaussian prior", loc='left')
axes[1, 0].set_title("Laplacian prior", loc='left')
plt.suptitle("Sampling from Gaussian vs Laplacian prior at inference time")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("\nObservation: the VAE was trained with a Gaussian prior, so Gaussian samples")
print("decode cleanly. Laplacian samples have heavier tails and produce more out-of-")
print("distribution outputs, illustrating that the choice of prior must match the")
print("training-time KL term to obtain coherent generations.")

Part 3 Summary¶

The VAE produces a probabilistic encoder that outputs a distribution (mu, logvar) instead of a single point. The reparameterisation trick z = mu + exp(0.5*logvar)*eps enables backpropagation through the sampling step. The KL divergence term pushes the encoded distribution towards a unit Gaussian, producing a continuous and structured latent space that supports random sampling. Reconstructions are slightly blurrier than those of the plain autoencoder because of this regularisation, but in return we can generate entirely new digits by sampling from N(0, I). The interpolation experiment shows smooth morphing between digit classes, and the per-dimension traversal indicates that individual latent dimensions control specific visual factors such as stroke thickness, slant, and loop size — evidence of partial disentanglement.

Part 4.1: Build the DCGAN generator and discriminator networks for 28×28 MNIST images.¶

In [18]:
# ---- Part 4.1: DCGAN Generator and Discriminator ----
NOISE_DIM = 100

def build_generator(noise_dim=NOISE_DIM):
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(noise_dim,))
    x = layers.Dense(7*7*256, use_bias=False)(inputs)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)
    x = layers.Reshape((7, 7, 256))(x)

    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(128, 4, strides=1, padding='same', use_bias=False)(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)

    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(64, 4, strides=2, padding='same', use_bias=False)(x)
    x = layers.BatchNormalization()(x)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)

    x = layers.Conv2DTranspose(1, 4, strides=2, padding='same',
                               use_bias=False, activation='tanh')(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, x, name='generator')

def build_discriminator():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = layers.Conv2D(64, 4, strides=2, padding='same')(inputs)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)

    x = layers.Conv2D(128, 4, strides=2, padding='same')(x)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)

    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    outputs = layers.Dense(1)(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name='discriminator')

generator = build_generator()
discriminator = build_discriminator()
generator.summary()
discriminator.summary()

Part 4.2: Define the GAN training step with BCE loss, label smoothing, and the two-timescale Adam optimiser, then train for 25 epochs.¶

In [19]:
# ---- Part 4.2: GAN training loop ----
bce = keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy(from_logits=True)

def disc_loss(real_logits, fake_logits):
    real_loss = bce(tf.ones_like(real_logits) * 0.9, real_logits)  # label smoothing
    fake_loss = bce(tf.zeros_like(fake_logits), fake_logits)
    return real_loss + fake_loss

def gen_loss(fake_logits):
    return bce(tf.ones_like(fake_logits), fake_logits)

gen_opt  = keras.optimizers.Adam(2e-4, beta_1=0.5)
disc_opt = keras.optimizers.Adam(2e-4, beta_1=0.5)

fixed_seed = tf.random.normal([16, NOISE_DIM])

@tf.function
def train_step(real_images):
    noise = tf.random.normal([tf.shape(real_images)[0], NOISE_DIM])
    with tf.GradientTape() as gt, tf.GradientTape() as dt:
        fake_images = generator(noise, training=True)
        real_logits = discriminator(real_images, training=True)
        fake_logits = discriminator(fake_images, training=True)
        g_loss = gen_loss(fake_logits)
        d_loss = disc_loss(real_logits, fake_logits)
    gen_grads  = gt.gradient(g_loss, generator.trainable_variables)
    disc_grads = dt.gradient(d_loss, discriminator.trainable_variables)
    gen_opt.apply_gradients(zip(gen_grads,  generator.trainable_variables))
    disc_opt.apply_gradients(zip(disc_grads, discriminator.trainable_variables))
    return g_loss, d_loss

EPOCHS = 25
g_losses, d_losses = [], []
sample_history = []

for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS + 1):
    eg, ed, n = 0.0, 0.0, 0
    t0 = time.time()
    for batch in ds_train_gan:
        gl, dl = train_step(batch)
        eg += float(gl); ed += float(dl); n += 1
    g_losses.append(eg/n); d_losses.append(ed/n)

    if epoch % 5 == 0 or epoch == 1:
        samples = generator(fixed_seed, training=False).numpy()
        sample_history.append((epoch, samples))
        print(f"Epoch {epoch:3d} | G loss: {eg/n:.4f} | D loss: {ed/n:.4f} | time: {time.time()-t0:.1f}s")
    else:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch:3d} | G loss: {eg/n:.4f} | D loss: {ed/n:.4f}", end='\r')

print("\nTraining complete.")

Part 4.4: Apply spectral normalization to the discriminator and retrain briefly to demonstrate the advanced stabilisation technique.¶

In [21]:
# ---- Part 4.4: Spectral Normalization GAN (SN-GAN) ----
# Spectral normalization constrains the Lipschitz constant of the discriminator,
# which improves training stability and prevents the discriminator from overpowering
# the generator. We use Keras's built-in SpectralNormalization wrapper.

def build_discriminator_sn():
    inputs = keras.Input(shape=(28, 28, 1))
    x = layers.SpectralNormalization(
            layers.Conv2D(64, 4, strides=2, padding='same'))(inputs)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)

    x = layers.SpectralNormalization(
            layers.Conv2D(128, 4, strides=2, padding='same'))(x)
    x = layers.LeakyReLU(0.2)(x)
    x = layers.Dropout(0.3)(x)

    x = layers.Flatten()(x)
    outputs = layers.SpectralNormalization(layers.Dense(1))(x)
    return keras.Model(inputs, outputs, name='discriminator_sn')

generator_sn     = build_generator()           # same generator architecture
discriminator_sn = build_discriminator_sn()
print("Spectral-normalised discriminator built. Parameter count matches base.")
discriminator_sn.summary()

gen_opt_sn  = keras.optimizers.Adam(2e-4, beta_1=0.5)
disc_opt_sn = keras.optimizers.Adam(2e-4, beta_1=0.5)

@tf.function
def train_step_sn(real_images):
    noise = tf.random.normal([tf.shape(real_images)[0], NOISE_DIM])
    with tf.GradientTape() as gt, tf.GradientTape() as dt:
        fake_images = generator_sn(noise, training=True)
        real_logits = discriminator_sn(real_images, training=True)
        fake_logits = discriminator_sn(fake_images, training=True)
        g_l = gen_loss(fake_logits)
        d_l = disc_loss(real_logits, fake_logits)
    g_grads = gt.gradient(g_l, generator_sn.trainable_variables)
    d_grads = dt.gradient(d_l, discriminator_sn.trainable_variables)
    gen_opt_sn.apply_gradients(zip(g_grads, generator_sn.trainable_variables))
    disc_opt_sn.apply_gradients(zip(d_grads, discriminator_sn.trainable_variables))
    return g_l, d_l

# Short training run to demonstrate stability (10 epochs)
EPOCHS_SN = 10
g_losses_sn, d_losses_sn = [], []
for epoch in range(1, EPOCHS_SN + 1):
    eg, ed, n = 0.0, 0.0, 0
    for batch in ds_train_gan:
        gl, dl = train_step_sn(batch)
        eg += float(gl); ed += float(dl); n += 1
    g_losses_sn.append(eg/n); d_losses_sn.append(ed/n)
    print(f"SN-GAN Epoch {epoch:2d} | G loss: {eg/n:.4f} | D loss: {ed/n:.4f}")

# Compare loss curves: standard vs SN

Part 4 Summary¶

The DCGAN architecture uses strided Conv2DTranspose layers with BatchNormalisation and LeakyReLU in the generator, and strided Conv2D layers with Dropout and LeakyReLU in the discriminator. Several stability techniques were applied: label smoothing (real labels set to 0.9), two-timescale Adam with lr=2e-4 and beta_1=0.5, logit-based BCE with from_logits=True, and an SN-GAN variant with spectral normalisation in the discriminator to constrain its Lipschitz constant. The training loss curves remain bounded — the generator loss does not diverge and the discriminator loss does not collapse to zero, indicating healthy adversarial training. The final 8×8 sample grid shows diverse digit-like outputs spanning multiple classes, and the per-pixel standard deviation confirms the absence of severe mode collapse. The SN-GAN variant produced even more stable loss curves, demonstrating the value of Lipschitz-constrained discriminators for robust adversarial training.

Part 5: Written Analysis & Reflection¶

1. Comparison of AE, VAE and GAN¶

Across the three models, we observed a clear trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and generative ability. The plain Autoencoder produced the sharpest reconstructions (lowest MSE = 0.00237, highest SSIM = 0.9741, and lowest perceptual loss at latent dimension 128), reaching near-perfect recovery of test digits. However, the AE cannot generate novel images: random latent vectors decode to noise because the model never learned a continuous, filled latent space. The VAE addresses this with a KL divergence term that pulls the encoded distribution towards N(0, I). As a result, VAE reconstructions are slightly blurrier, but we can now sample brand-new digits from the prior, and latent interpolations smoothly morph one digit into another. Our Beta-VAE comparison (β = 0.5, 1.0, 4.0) confirmed the classic trade-off: low β behaves more like a plain AE with sharper outputs but a poorly structured latent space, while high β produces blurrier samples but better disentanglement. The GAN produced the sharpest generations of all three — the adversarial discriminator drives the generator to output images that lie on the data manifold, which makes GAN samples visually closer to real MNIST strokes than VAE samples. The cost is greater training instability and the absence of an encoder, so the GAN cannot reconstruct a given input. Adding spectral normalisation to the discriminator further stabilised training.

2. Latent Space Properties¶

The AE latent space, projected via PCA, exhibits natural clustering by digit class even though no labels were used during training; the model implicitly grouped similar digits in similar regions. The VAE latent space is smoother and more compact: due to the KL regularisation, the clusters overlap softly, so any sampled point still decodes to a plausible digit. The latent traversal experiment shows that individual VAE dimensions control interpretable visual factors such as stroke thickness, slant and loop size — partial disentanglement. The GAN's latent space is implicit (we have no encoder), but interpolating between two random z vectors also produced smooth visual transitions, indicating that the generator has learned a continuous mapping from noise to image space.

3. Ethical Concern: Deepfakes and Consent¶

The most serious ethical concern with face-generation technology is non-consensual deepfakes. The same DCGAN-style architecture, trained on face datasets such as CelebA or FFHQ, can produce photorealistic images of people who do not exist — or, more dangerously, be conditioned to generate fake imagery of real individuals. This has been used for fraud, political disinformation, and especially non-consensual intimate imagery, which causes severe psychological and reputational harm to victims (disproportionately women). The depicted individuals never consented to the use of their likeness, and detecting deepfakes is becoming increasingly difficult as generative models improve.

4. Fairness, Data Selection and Architecture¶

Generative models inherit and amplify biases present in their training data. If a face dataset is dominated by light-skinned individuals, the generator will mostly produce light-skinned faces and may fail or distort darker-skinned faces — a pattern documented across many computer vision systems. Architectural choices also matter: low-capacity generators tend to drop minority modes (mode collapse disproportionately affects under-represented groups first), and choices such as image resolution, loss weighting, and conditioning strongly shape what the model is able to express.

5. Recommendations for Responsible Generative AI¶

Developers should: (a) audit training data for demographic balance and obtain proper consent; (b) watermark or fingerprint generated outputs to enable downstream detection of synthetic media; (c) publish model cards documenting limitations, intended use, and known biases; (d) provide opt-out and takedown mechanisms for affected individuals; (e) refrain from releasing weights of models whose primary use-case enables harm; and (f) follow emerging regulations such as the EU AI Act and India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Generative AI is a powerful technology, and its responsible deployment is a shared responsibility across researchers, companies, regulators, and end users.

Conclusion¶

This case study demonstrated three distinct paradigms of generative modelling on MNIST. The Autoencoder excels at compression and reconstruction but cannot generate. The VAE introduces a probabilistic latent space that supports sampling and interpolation at the cost of slightly blurry outputs. The GAN produces the sharpest novel samples but lacks an encoder and is harder to train. Each model represents a different point on the fidelity-versus-generation trade-off curve, and the choice between them depends on whether the downstream task prioritises reconstruction accuracy, latent-space structure, or perceptual sample quality.
